extracted.intended_audience: general public; readers interested in media, journalism, and Pulitzer Prize controversies
extracted.subtask_description: News coverage about the Pulitzer Prize Board's review of a past award (Walter Duranty, 1932), discussing the board's procedures, historical precedent, and journalistic standards implicated by calls for revocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board review intent and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The review 'is intended to seriously consider all relevant information regarding Mr. Duranty's award.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review is being handled by a board subcommittee; 'all aspects and ramifications will be considered.' The board treats significant complaints seriously and will analyze the factors that must be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of written revocation procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no written procedures regarding prize revocation. There are no standards or precedents for revoking the prize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because formal procedures/standards do not exist, the board says 'We look at what would be reasonable and analyze the factors that would have to be considered.' This implies case-by-case judgment rather than a codified rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal scope of the prize (single-year recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Pulitzer Prize recognizes the work during a single year rather than 'a winner's body of work over time.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The board emphasized that the 1932 prize honored Duranty's stories from the previous year, which the board says were unrelated to the famine—implying evaluations should focus on the specific work for which the prize was given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical precedent on revocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the creation of the Pulitzer Prize in 1917, the board has never revoked an award.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Past reconsiderations (e.g., 1990 decision against withdrawing Duranty's honor) and the longstanding absence of revocations are relevant context; the board looks to precedent even though no formal precedent for revocation exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serious misconduct — fabrication as grounds for return/revocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Fabrication is treated as serious misconduct (example: in 1981, The Washington Post returned a Pulitzer awarded to Janet Cooke, a reporter who fabricated a story).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Cooke case is cited as an example of severe falsification leading to return of a prize; fabrication is thus an explicit category of misconduct the board (and institutions) respond to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic objectivity and accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholars and other journalists have repeatedly questioned the objectivity and accuracy of Duranty's work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critiques include that Duranty 'reported Communist Party propaganda rather than the facts of daily life' and that his coverage has been 'discredited' by later reporting; objectivity and factual accuracy are core evaluative criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to report atrocities (omission of famine/genocide)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics (including the UCCA) contend Duranty 'not only disregarded the famine-genocide in his dispatches but called other journalists outright liars' for reporting on the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omission of major human-rights atrocities or genocide in dispatches is presented as a substantive failure that can prompt calls for revocation or review; timing of the reporting and relation to awarded work are relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict between access and truthful reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Accusations that Duranty preserved his special access to Stalin by not reporting on the famine (S.J. Taylor's claim that he 'knew of the famine ... but did not report on it to preserve his special access to Stalin').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This highlights an evaluative standard concerning whether a journalist compromised reporting integrity to maintain access—such conflicts may weigh against the quality/ethics of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance of awarded work vs later-discredited coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: The board noted that the stories for which Duranty was honored were 'unrelated to the famine' and emphasized the prize recognizes specific year's work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This establishes a criterion that later-discredited reporting on other events may be considered differently than the specific work that earned the prize; the relation between criticized conduct and the awarded material matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public petitions and external pressure as triggers
rubrics_metrics.description: A massive campaign (more than 15,000 postcards and thousands of letters and e-mails) by Ukrainians and organizations urged the board to revoke Duranty's prize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While public campaigns can trigger or intensify reviews, the board states it had decided to review before most mail arrived; nevertheless, volume of external complaints is acknowledged as a factor prompting examination.
